subject: Conduit selection: on-prem hubsite -> cloud (peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S)
messages:
From: Derek Hunter <derek.hunter@acme-analytics.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>
Cc: Sarah Choi <sarah.choi@edgecloud.io>
Date: 2027-05-29T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Quick ask: best link pattern for our hub-site -> Redwood Private deployment

Jordan —

Thanks again for the intro call yesterday. Our infra team at Acme is evaluating how to attach our single on-prem 'hub' datacenter to Redwood Private (you noted we can do VPC peering, PrivateLink-style endpoint, or a site-to-site VPN). We primarily care about: predictable latency for inference (p95), operational simplicity for our ops team, and minimizing egress complexity across multiple cloud regions.

Attached is a simple diagram (network-diagram-v2.png) and a CSV with sample latency measurements to your hosted edge (s2s-latency-sample.csv). High-level questions:
- From Redwoods' side, which pattern do you recommend for a single on-prem hub that will serve multiple regional services?
- Any gotchas with PrivateLink (service endpoints) and multi-region fanout?
- If we go peering, will cross-account VPC peering limit routing options for our security appliances?

Would appreciate a concise recommendation and a short mutual action plan so we can push this through our architects.

Thanks,
Derek
Derek Hunter
Head of Platform Engineering | Acme Analytics

Subject: Re: Quick ask: best link pattern for our hub-site -> Redwood Private deployment

Derek —

Thanks for the diagram and latency samples, that helps. Quick high-level reply below; I looped in Karthik (network architect) and Neha (product / Private deployment lead) for details. Sarah — appreciate EdgeCloud perspective if you have any field notes.

Short answer: there is no one-size-fits-all. For a single on-prem hub that fans out to multiple cloud regions, we typically recommend either a PrivateLink-like approach (regional endpoint per cloud region with a small control plane) or a well-provisioned S2S VPN if you need simple central control and are comfortable with the latency profile. VPC peering can be fine but becomes operationally brittle as you add regions/accounts.

I'm attaching a simple cost/ops checklist we use (privatelink-cost-estimate.xlsx). Karthik — can you draft a short technical pros/cons matrix (latency, maintenance, routing complexity, failure modes) for the three options? Neha — please add any product constraints (SLA, supported topologies) we should call out for Acme's decision doc.

Proposed next steps (mutual action plan):
1) Redwood provides concise pros/cons + recommended default for hub-fanout (by EOD).
2) Acme confirms whether the hub will do NAT/egress and whether security appliances must inspect egress.
3) If PrivateLink recommended, we create a regional endpoint rollout plan; if S2S chosen, we prepare VPN config + throughput targets.

Jordan
Jordan Blake
Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>, Derek Hunter <derek.hunter@acme-analytics.com>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-05-29T11:27:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Quick ask: best link pattern for our hub-site -> Redwood Private deployment

Derek / Jordan —

Below is a compact tech matrix from the infra perspective. I've kept it focused on measurable differences.

Option A: PrivateLink / Endpoint per region (recommended when low blast radius + controlled egress required)
- Latency: typically lowest intra-region; cross-region fanout requires your hub to forward to other regions (adds RTT). For single-region heavy traffic, this is excellent.
- Ops: requires provisioning endpoints per region and managing acceptance; moderate complexity.
- Routing: keeps traffic inside service endpoints; avoids modifying VPC route tables for each peer.
- Failure modes: endpoint availability and cross-region forwarding complexity.
- Security: supports least privilege; you can restrict endpoints to specific principals.
- Cost: per-endpoint charges + data processing costs (see attached estimate).

Option B: Site-to-Site VPN (centralized hub VPN)
- Latency: depends on your VPN endpoint. If you have a well-provisioned appliance with fast routes to multiple clouds, p95 can be acceptable for many inference workloads, but jitter/policy churn can be higher than PrivateLink.
- Ops: simpler for a single hub — one tunnel pair to manage, centralized security inspection possible.
- Routing: you control all routing from your hub; simpler to apply NAT/inspection.
- Failure modes: tunnel flaps; throughput limits per tunnel (need HA pairs).
- Security: inspection is straightforward; however, multi-tenant cloud egress may require additional ACLs.

Option C: Cross-account VPC Peering (not recommended for multi-region fanout)
- Latency: low inside a single VPC-to-VPC peer within same region.
- Ops: management explosion as you add peers; route table sprawl and limitations on transitive routing make it awkward for a hub that fans out.
- Routing: no transitive peering — your hub would need additional proxies; complicates security appliances.
- Failure modes: many point-to-point links to monitor.

My pragmatic recommendation:
- If Acme wants centralized inspection/NAT and a single operational control point, choose S2S VPN with HA tunnels and provisioned throughput; pair with BGP for failover.
- If low-latency per-region inference matters most and you can accept multiple endpoints, choose PrivateLink per-region and push logic to a regional forwarding layer in your hub.
- Avoid cross-account peering if you plan to support >2 regions or expect frequent account topology changes.

I'll attach a small checklist for VPN HA sizing if you want (I can follow up with numbers).

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Network Architect | Redwood Inference

From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>

Date: 2027-05-29T13:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Quick ask: best link pattern for our hub-site -> Redwood Private deployment

Derek —

Adding product constraints and support notes so Acme has a clear operational picture:
- Redwood Private supports both endpoint-style ingress and S2S VPNs. For PrivateLink-like endpoints we require an acceptance flow per region (we have an API/quasi-automated flow that reduces manual steps).
- SLA: our SLA applies to the compute/service once traffic hits the regional control plane. Network path SLAs depend on your chosen connectivity (we can include a runbook for failover).
- Auditing: if you need audit logs for token-level access and per-request tracing across regions, PrivateLink makes it easier to centralize logs per-region. For S2S we recommend instrumenting the hub appliance to forward logs to our ingestion pipeline.
- Billing: endpoint egress and per-endpoint costs apply for PrivateLink; S2S will shift costs to Acme's egress/peering arrangements.

Operational callouts:
- If Acme requires deep packet inspection or central IDS, S2S is simpler.
- If you need to scale independently by region (separate teams/SLAs), PrivateLink avoids cross-account routing changes.

If this aligns with your preference, Jordan and I can draft the final recommendation and an ops checklist for your runbook.

-Neha
Neha Kapoor
Product Lead, Private Deployments | Redwood Inference

Next actions from Acme:
- We will confirm expected sustained throughput and spike requirements (ETA: Tue).
- We'll provide contact for our network appliance vendor so Karthik can size HA tunnels.

Would Redwood be able to draft a short VPN HA sizing doc and an S2S config example (BGP, IP ranges, MTU recommendations)? If so, let's schedule a 30-minute follow-up early next week to finalize.

Appreciate the quick turnaround.
